questions.question: In `data Result = Pass | Fail`, what is `Pass`?
options: A type
A data constructor — a value of type Result
A type class
A module
questions.explanation: Pass and Fail are data constructors: the actual values a Result can take. Result is the type; Pass and Fail are values of that type, which is why they are capitalised like every other constructor.
optionFeedback: Result is the type. Pass is one of the values that type can hold — a constructor, not a type itself.
Correct — Pass and Fail are data constructors, the values of the Result type, exactly like True and False are the values of Bool.
A type class is a set of operations a type may support (Chapter 9). Pass carries no operations; it is a value.
Modules group definitions together (next chapter); Pass is a value, not a unit of code organisation.

questions.question: `describe` pattern matches `Pass` and `Fail` and nothing else. Why does GHC accept this as complete?
options: GHC does not check completeness for custom types
Because a wildcard pattern is implied
Because Result has exactly two constructors, and both are covered
Because Pass and Fail derive Bounded
questions.explanation: An enumeration's constructors are the only possible values of the type. Matching every constructor — here, both Pass and Fail — covers every case, so the match is exhaustive with no wildcard needed.
optionFeedback: GHC does check, and with -Wincomplete-patterns will warn about a missing constructor case — it just has nothing to warn about here.
No wildcard is present or needed; the two explicit patterns already account for every constructor.
Correct — Result has exactly two constructors, Pass and Fail, and the function has one equation for each, so nothing is left uncovered.
Bounded is unrelated to pattern-match exhaustiveness; it is about minBound/maxBound, covered in Chapter 9.

questions.question: `print (classify 64)` fails with `No instance for (Show Result)`. What is missing?
options: A type annotation on classify
deriving (Show) on the Result declaration
An import of Prelude
A pattern match for every constructor
questions.explanation: print needs Show a => a -> IO (), and GHC does not invent a Show instance on its own for a type you declared. Adding deriving (Show) asks it to generate one.
optionFeedback: classify already has a correct signature; the problem is that Result has no Show instance, not that its type is unannotated.
Correct — GHC will not print a value unless its type derives (or defines) Show. Add deriving (Show) to the data declaration.
Prelude is imported automatically into every module (covered next chapter); the missing piece is an instance, not an import.
classify already pattern matches exhaustively; that is unrelated to whether Result can be printed.

questions.question: Given `data Result = Pass | Fail deriving (Ord)`, why is `Pass < Fail` True rather than False?
options: Pass is alphabetically before Fail
Derived Ord orders constructors by their declaration order, and Pass is declared first
Ord always orders True-like values first
It is arbitrary and could change between compilations
questions.explanation: A derived Ord instance ranks constructors purely by the order they appear in the data declaration — first declared is smallest. Pass appears before Fail, so Pass < Fail.
optionFeedback: Alphabetical order is a coincidence here — P does not come before F alphabetically, so that cannot be the rule. The real rule is declaration order.
Correct — deriving Ord ranks constructors by declaration order: Pass was written first, so it compares as smaller.
Ord has no notion of 'True-like'; that is not how the derivation works for an arbitrary enumeration.
It is fixed by the order written in the source file, not arbitrary — recompiling without changing the declaration gives the same result every time.

questions.question: What is the type of the Rectangle constructor, given `data Shape = Circle Float | Rectangle Float Float`?
options: Shape
Float -> Shape
Float -> Float -> Shape
(Float, Float) -> Shape
questions.explanation: Rectangle takes two Floats before it produces a Shape, so like any two-argument curried function its type is Float -> Float -> Shape.
optionFeedback: Shape is the type of a fully applied Rectangle value, e.g. Rectangle 3.0 4.0 — but the constructor itself is a function, not a finished value.
That is Circle's type. Rectangle takes two Floats, not one, so it needs a second arrow.
Correct — Rectangle is curried, exactly like any other two-argument function: Float -> Float -> Shape.
That would be the type if Rectangle took one tupled argument. It takes two separate curried Float arguments, not a pair.

questions.question: Why does `area (Circle r) = pi * r * r` need parentheses around `Circle r`?
options: Parentheses are only a style preference here
Because function application binds tighter than a constructor pattern, so `area Circle r` would parse as area given two separate arguments
Because Circle is a type, not a constructor
Because pi requires parentheses
questions.explanation: Without parentheses, area Circle r would be read as area applied to two separate arguments, Circle and r, the same left-associative rule that makes ordinary application group tightly. Parentheses group Circle r into a single pattern that area's one argument matches against.
optionFeedback: It is required, not stylistic — omitting it changes how the equation parses, giving area the wrong number of arguments.
Correct — application is left-associative and binds tightly, so area Circle r would parse as area given two arguments; (Circle r) groups the constructor and its field into one pattern.
Circle is the constructor here; Shape is the type. Either way this is not why parentheses are needed.
pi is a plain numeric constant used inside the function body; it has nothing to do with the parentheses around the pattern.

questions.question: Why does `Metres 100 + Feet 30` fail under newtype, just as it did under data?
options: newtype secretly compiles down to data with extra checks
newtype still creates a genuinely distinct type at compile time, even though the wrapper vanishes at run time
Metres and Feet do not derive Num
newtype forbids arithmetic entirely
questions.explanation: The compile-time type checker sees Metres and Feet as fully distinct types under newtype, exactly as under data — that is what rejects the mismatched addition. What newtype changes is only what happens after type checking succeeds: no wrapper survives into the compiled program.
optionFeedback: It is not a shortcut for data with extra checks; it is its own mechanism that is erased after type checking, unlike data which keeps a real runtime structure.
Correct — type separation is a compile-time property. newtype keeps that separation exactly like data, and only removes the run-time representation.
True, but beside the point — the error reported is a type mismatch between Metres and Feet, which would be reported before Num was ever checked, exactly as the data version showed.
newtype does not forbid arithmetic; it forbids nothing that data would not also forbid. Mixing two distinct types is what fails, not arithmetic itself.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid reason to choose newtype over data for `Metres`?
options: Metres needs several fields
Metres needs to be recursive
Metres wraps exactly one Double and needs no extra structure — only type-level separation
Metres needs more than one constructor
questions.explanation: newtype is for the specific case of one constructor wrapping one field, used purely to keep two otherwise-identical types apart. Anything beyond that — more fields, more constructors, recursion — needs data.
optionFeedback: Several fields would need data; newtype allows exactly one field.
Recursion would need data; newtype's single-field, single-constructor shape cannot express it.
Correct — this is exactly the case newtype is for: one value, wrapped only to get type-level separation, at no run-time cost.
More than one constructor would need data; newtype allows exactly one.

questions.question: What does newtype keep from data, and what does it give up in exchange?
options: It keeps genuine type-level separation (mixing two newtypes is still a compile error) but gives up generality — exactly one constructor, exactly one field, no recursion
It keeps the extra run-time structure of data but gives up compile-time type checking entirely
It keeps everything data offers, with no trade-off at all
It gives up type-level separation in exchange for zero run-time cost
questions.explanation: newtype Metres = Metres Double still rejects Metres 100 + Feet 30 at compile time, exactly like data would — that separation is not given up. What is given up is data's extra flexibility: newtype cannot have more than one constructor, more than one field, or be recursive.
optionFeedback: Correct — the type checker still keeps Metres and Feet apart; the trade-off is purely about structural generality, not about safety.
This has it backwards on both counts: newtype keeps compile-time checking and gives up run-time structure (the wrapper is erased), not the reverse.
There is a genuine trade-off — newtype cannot express several fields, several constructors, or recursion, unlike data.
Type-level separation is exactly what newtype keeps; it is the run-time wrapper, not the safety, that disappears.

questions.question: Why is newtype Shape = Circle Float | Rectangle Float Float rejected by GHC?
options: newtype allows only one constructor with exactly one field; GHC needs there to be exactly one way to build and unwrap the value to erase the wrapper safely
Float is not a valid field type for newtype
Shape is already the name of a built-in type
newtype requires every field to be named, as in record syntax
questions.explanation: The Common Mistake box states this directly: newtype needs exactly one constructor and exactly one field so that the compiler can erase the wrapper completely at compile time. Two constructors (Circle and Rectangle) or a constructor with two fields (Rectangle's pair of Floats) both break that requirement.
optionFeedback: Correct — the restriction is structural (one constructor, one field), not about which types can appear inside.
Float is used freely elsewhere as a newtype's field, e.g. newtype Metres = Metres Double works the same way with Double.
Shape is not a reserved or built-in name; the rejection has nothing to do with naming, only with structure.
Field names are optional for both data and newtype — this declaration is positional, and that is not the reason it fails.

questions.question: Given `data Student = Student { studentName :: String, studentMark :: Int, isActive :: Bool }`, what does GHC generate automatically?
options: Nothing extra; you must still write pattern matches to read fields
A function per field, e.g. studentName :: Student -> String, studentMark :: Student -> Int
A JSON serialiser for Student
A default value for every unset field
questions.explanation: Record syntax's main practical benefit is that GHC generates one accessor function per named field, with the type Student -> FieldType. That is what makes studentName kago valid without a hand-written pattern match.
optionFeedback: This is exactly what record syntax avoids — that manual work is what positional constructors like StudentP require.
Correct — one accessor function is generated per field, letting you call studentMark kago directly instead of pattern matching.
Haskell's derived Show produces a readable String representation, not JSON, and record syntax has nothing to do with serialisation formats.
Every field must still be supplied when a Student is constructed; record syntax does not introduce defaults.

questions.question: What does `kago { studentMark = 75 }` actually do?
options: Changes kago's mark field in place
Builds and returns a new Student, copying every other field from kago
Fails to compile, because Student already has a value for studentMark
Deletes kago and replaces it globally
questions.explanation: Record update syntax constructs a fresh value that copies every field from the original except the ones named, which take the new values instead. kago itself is never modified — there is no mutation in pure Haskell.
optionFeedback: There is no in-place mutation in Haskell; kago keeps its original studentMark unless you reassign the name to a new value.
Correct — this expression evaluates to a brand-new Student value with studentMark replaced and everything else copied from kago.
This compiles and is the normal, idiomatic way to produce a modified copy of a record value.
Nothing is deleted or replaced globally; kago still exists with its original fields unless you rebind the name yourself.

questions.question: Why can a data declaration be recursive when a type synonym cannot?
options: data declarations are compiled, type synonyms are not
A constructor like Branch or Cons stops the expansion; a synonym has nothing to stop it expanding forever
Recursive types are a special case handled outside the type system
type synonyms can be recursive too, but only with two type parameters
questions.explanation: type Chain = [Chain] would need to be expanded forever to know what Chain is, with no base case. A data declaration's constructors are themselves complete, finite descriptions: Branch (Tree a) (Tree a) just holds two Trees without needing to expand Tree any further to type-check.
optionFeedback: Both data declarations and type synonyms are compiled; that is not the distinguishing factor.

Correct — a constructor is a stopping point. GHC does not need to expand Tree further to know Branch (Tree a) (Tree a) is well formed; a synonym has no such stopping point and would expand without end.
There is nothing special-cased here — it follows directly from what a constructor is, the same mechanism used throughout this section.
Recursive type synonyms are rejected regardless of how many parameters they take; parameter count is not the issue.

questions.question: In `countLeaves (Branch l r) = countLeaves l + countLeaves r`, what stops the recursion from running forever?
options: The + operator has a built-in limit
GHC detects infinite recursion at compile time and rejects it
Every Branch eventually leads to Leaf values, which match the base-case equation instead of recursing further
countLeaves is memoised automatically
questions.explanation: A Tree built with finitely many Branch and Leaf constructors is finite by construction. Each recursive call moves to a strictly smaller subtree, and every path through a finite tree eventually reaches a Leaf, which countLeaves handles without calling itself again — the same base-case discipline as Chapter 5's recursion on lists.
optionFeedback: + is ordinary arithmetic with no awareness of recursion or termination; it just adds the two results once they exist.
GHC does not perform general termination checking; recursion terminates here because of the data's finite structure, not a compiler guarantee.
Correct — a finite tree has finitely many Branch levels before reaching a Leaf, and the Leaf equation is a base case with no recursive call.
Nothing here is memoised; countLeaves recomputes from scratch on each call, exactly as written.
